Paint and overspray removal, and what it landed on

Spray drift from a neighbour's job, splatter from a repaint, roller spots across a driveway, or a line of overspray down a fence. The combination of paint type and substrate decides whether this is ten minutes or whether it is not worth attempting, and that is settled by a test patch rather than by a guess. The test patch is free and the removal is quoted per panel from a photograph of the affected area.

  • Test patch before anything is applied
  • Never a solvent on an unknown coating
  • Sometimes repainting is the better option

Why it is a combination problem

A solvent that removes paint works by attacking a binder. The trouble is that most of the surfaces paint lands on also have a binder: the acrylic in a render, the resin in a powder coat, the sealer on a driveway, the paint already on a fence.

So the question is never just what the overspray is. It is whether there is a product that attacks the overspray faster than it attacks what is underneath, and enough of a margin between the two to work in. On glass and dense concrete there is plenty of margin. On powder coated aluminium or a painted weatherboard there may be almost none, and sometimes touching up is cheaper than removing.

The combinations

What is realistic on each surface

Expected outcome where the overspray is recent. Everything here gets harder with time and sun.
  Approach Realistic outcome
Glass Blade and solvent, with the glass checked for fabricating debris first Full removal, reliably. The best case there is
Smooth concrete and precast Solvent with dwell, light mechanical work Usually full. Dense surfaces hold very little
Exposed aggregate and porous concrete Solvent, dwell, sometimes repeated Good. A faint shadow in the pores is possible
Face brick Solvent worked from the edge inward Usually good. Very porous brick can keep a ghost
Render and texture coat Gentlest product, tested, mechanical kept minimal Variable. Textured render holds paint in the profile
Powder coated aluminium Specific product, tested on a hidden section Often good. The wrong product strips the coating, so this is tested every time
Colorbond As for powder coat, carefully Usually good. The coating warranty is worth more than the saving
Painted timber and weatherboard Mechanical only, very carefully Poor. Touching up is usually cheaper and better
Decking and raw timber Absorbed into the grain Sanding, which is a different trade. We will say so

The test patch is free and it is not a formality

On paint removal the test patch is doing real work: it establishes whether there is a usable margin between the overspray and the surface under it. We pick somewhere you will not look, treat it, and show you. If the margin is too narrow we will tell you that removal is likely to do more harm than the overspray, and you have paid nothing to find out. Send a photo of the affected panel and the test patch is arranged before anything is charged: Start a quote or call 0400 638 010.

Questions

Asked about overspray

A neighbour's spray drifted onto my car and my windows. Can you help?

Glass yes, and usually completely. Vehicle paintwork is a different trade and we would send you to a detailer rather than attempt it, because automotive clear coat has its own products and its own risks.

Windows, frames, fencing, driveway and render we can look at. Photograph everything before anyone touches it, which matters if it becomes an insurance conversation.

How long do I have before it is too late?

The sooner the better, and sun is the accelerator. Fresh overspray on glass or dense concrete comes off easily for weeks. The same drift after a hot Melbourne summer has cured hard and, on porous surfaces, migrated into the pores.

Days matter more than weeks on textured and porous surfaces.

Can you remove paint without damaging the surface underneath?

On glass, dense concrete and brick, almost always. On render, powder coat and painted surfaces it depends entirely on whether there is a margin between the two coatings, which is exactly what the test patch establishes.

Where there is no margin we will tell you before anything is applied.

What about paint on my driveway?

Usually removable. Water based paint on unsealed concrete comes off well. Oil based and two pack are harder, and a sealed driveway is actually the easy case because the paint sat on the sealer rather than going into the slab.

Large areas of roller splatter are often better handled by cleaning the whole driveway afterwards so the treated area does not stand out.

Should I try a paint stripper from the hardware store?

On glass, carefully, yes. On anything else, we would not. Hardware strippers are formulated to remove architectural paint and they do not distinguish between the overspray and the render, the powder coat or the sealer underneath it.

The jobs that are genuinely difficult to fix are usually the ones where something aggressive was tried first.
